newsitem.title: ROMANIA: Judges challenge key Romania-Ukraine pact.
newsitem.headline: Judges challenge key Romania-Ukraine pact.

text.p: A key treaty between Romania and Ukraine, praised by President Bill Clinton during his visit to Bucharest last week, ran into a legal challenge on Tuesday over disputes dating from World War Two.

Officials at Romania's Supreme Court confirmed that they had issued a challenge to the treaty signed last month by the presidents of Romania and Ukraine after three years of often difficult talks and approved by the Bucharest parliament.

Seventeen of 34 Supreme Court judges, sitting last Friday during Clinton's eight-hour visit, said the treaty violated the 1991 constitution which proclaims Romania a "national, sovereign, independent, unitary and indivisible state".
The treaty with Ukraine, and a similar pact signed with Hungary last year, ended generations of mistrust and were key points in promoting Romania's bid for quick entry to NATO.
Although they failed to secure early membership at last week's Madrid summit, both Romania and Slovenia were singled out as prime candidates for a review of enlargements in 1999.

Addressing tens of thousands of Romanians apparently unbowed by the setback in Madrid, Clinton said: "You turned old grievances to new friendships within your borders and beyond. You have forged landmark treaties with Hungary and Ukraine."
In approaching the Constitutional Court, Romania's highest arbiter on legislation, the judges said the treaty made no claim to a tiny Black Sea island disputed for decades.

It further violated Romanian law by omitting a Ukrainian denunciation of the 1939 Nazi-Soviet pact which carved up eastern Europe between Hitler's Germany and the Kremlin. Large chunks of Romanian territory were seized by the Soviet Union.

There was no indication when the Constitutional Court would consider the matter. A Court spokesman said the case had little hope of success as it was submitted after Romanian President Emil Constantinescu had signed it into law.
"This submission is too late, it must have been a mistake by the court," he said.
Constantinescu and the new centrist government had made improved ties with Ukraine a foreign policy plank after treaty talks were blocked by their leftist predecessors.
His administration renounced claims to Serpent Island and both sides agreed to pursue separate talks on Black Sea borders to take account of important oil and gas deposits.

Leftists voted against ratification, along with the handful of Romanian nationalists in the parliament. Talks on similar post-Communist treaties with Russia and Moldova have stalled over similar disputes rooted in regional history.

The Interfax Ukraine news agency said a Romanian diplomat had asked the Kiev parliament to speed up ratification of the pact. The head of parliament's Foreign Affairs Committee, Borys Oliynyk, told Reuters the pact was unlikely to encounter any opposition when considered, probably in September.
